dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Immediately read both fixtures' next-shims.d.ts, package.json, vite.config.ts and next.config to establish the module contract before coding — grounds shims in the fixtures' declared signatures.
Read plugin-rsc dist .d.ts contract files (index.d.ts, rsc.d.ts, plugin-K7i9F4Fd.d.ts) and plugin internals to understand the RSC/Vite plugin API surface being wrapped.
Mapped vendored Next source to subsystems: read next/link, navigation, headers, cache, after, plus next-source TS for dev/build/start CLI and server — systematic subsystem-to-source mapping.

Reference consultation ceases entirely at step 39; ~300 debugging steps (including being stuck at 0/325 tests) proceed with NO re-consultation of vendored source when behavior turned ambiguous — the agent iterated on URL formats and process-killing instead of returning to source.

Only step touching use-cache/getStaticProps/middleware fixture files; no analysis note anywhere records non-obvious semantics (RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization), so contracts were inferred but subtle behaviors were not deliberately extracted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performed strong, systematic front-loaded research (steps 4-39): it read every fixture next-shims.d.ts, the plugin-rsc .d.ts contracts, and mapped vendored Next source to the required subsystems, clearly exceeding the level-5 anchor of merely reading the current subsystem's shims. However, it falls short of level 8 because research was entirely front-loaded and abandoned: across ~300 debugging steps it never re-consulted source to resolve ambiguous behavior (level-8's key trait) and recorded no non-obvious semantics like RSC boundaries or cache keys. This places it at 6 — well-targeted initial contract inference, but no sustained or self-correcting cross-referencing.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Identifies major subsystems (aliases/resolution, CLI dev/build/start, shims, SSR middleware, routing, after()) and states a sensible build order — package skeleton first, then plugin, then server features; a rough architecture rather than an undifferentiated push.

Partial vertical-slice attempt: gets dev server up, curls a single route, discovers 404, decides to implement SSR 'starting with pages router (pages-basic)' — dependency-aware ordering (resolution/plugin before routing before SSR) but no explicit done-criteria per milestone.

Plans are flat and repetitive — 'create all source files: plugin, CLI, shims, server, routing, build' mirroring the requirement bullets, no milestone gating or interface management between subsystems.

Back half collapses into hundreds of identical 'kill processes / rebuild / run tests' iterations; never reaches a testable state (0/325) and loses the milestone through-line, so no sustained living decomposition.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible dependency-aware order (resolution/plugin → dev server → SSR → routing), and briefly attempts a single-route vertical slice via manual curl (matching anchor 5). But it never produces an explicit milestone plan with done-criteria per subsystem, its planning is largely a flat list mirroring the requirements, and it lacks the test-gated, self-revising milestone structure of anchor 8 — the second half degenerates into an unstructured rebuild loop. This places the observed behavior at the level-5 anchor.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Read e2e spec files (cjs.spec, ssr.spec, routing-misc) early to understand what behavior tests check — reconnaissance of the ground-truth suite.

Stood up pages-basic fixture with `npx vinext dev` and curled `/` and `/about`; discovered all routes 404, correctly diagnosed missing SSR middleware and used that failure to drive the next implementation step — intermediate, failure-guided verification beyond pass/fail.
Repeated manual `timeout 8 npx vinext dev | head -20` probes on a single fixture to observe startup behavior, but these were largely defeated by a runaway background Vite process garbling output.
Ran the full run_tests.sh suite many times as a binary oracle, always reading only tail/grep of RESULTS; every run reported 0/325 and never triggered targeted subset runs.
At the end tests still show 0/325; never verified the production build/start path — dev itself never confirmed working, so no layered or build-path verification was achieved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent used the full suite mainly as a coarse pass/fail oracle (anchor 3) but did add genuine intermediate verification — standing up the pages-basic fixture manually and curling routes to observe SSR 404s and drive fixes — which lifts it above a pure 3. However, it never ran targeted Playwright subsets per subsystem, never confirmed the dev path actually worked (stuck at 0/325 throughout), and never exercised the production build/start path, so it falls well short of anchor 5's 'verifies dev and build paths work' with subset-guided fixes. This places the observed behavior at a 4.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: The one time it gets a real test signal: 0/325 passed because dev servers failed to start. This single datapoint anchors its entire mental model for the rest of the run.
A genuine manual probe (curl -> 404) confirming pages don't render — a small piece of real progress verification, but never expanded into per-subsystem tracking.
Repeatedly re-runs run_tests.sh to files but cannot read fresh results (garbled terminal); keeps citing the stale '0/325 passed' number rather than obtaining a current picture.

Dozens of near-identical analysis blocks restating the same '0/325 passed, dev servers failed to start' and the same root-cause list — clear evidence of looping on one failure without stepping back or re-baselining.
Submits 'task complete' while its own analysis still says 0/325 pass — no accurate done-vs-remaining reconciliation at the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent obtained essentially one real pass-rate signal (0/325) and a single curl probe, then spent the overwhelming majority of the horizon reactively looping on the same 'dev servers failed to start' failure, repeatedly parroting the stale count without ever re-establishing a current pass-rate or per-subsystem picture. It never detected it was circling, never quantified partial progress, and did no regression tracking — matching anchor 3 ('vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it'), lifted marginally above pure reactivity by its root-cause enumeration and lone verification probe, but far short of the level-5 behavior of tracking pass counts and re-checking after changes.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Genuine approach change: abandoned TypeScript source in favor of plain-JS files + copy build when TS compilation/npm install proved impossible offline. A real revision of the build/module strategy driven by falsified assumptions.

Reworked the plugin subsystem to add SSR middleware (route matching, ssrLoadModule, React render, head collection) after discovering the dev server returned 404 for all routes — a subsystem-level rework, though it was filling a missing piece rather than replacing a wrong design.
Adjusted plugin to load @vitejs/plugin-rsc/react from the app directory instead of vinext's own dir, and fixed bin path — local-to-medium fixes in response to server-start failures.

For ~150 steps stuck at 0/325 with servers not starting; repeatedly restates the same root causes ('catalog: protocol', 'no SSR middleware', 'ssrLoadModule path') and loops kill/rebuild/test without ever verifying a fix — circular re-patching, no foundational revision.

Repeats identical 'critical bugs' list (ssrLoadModule URL paths, shims, CLI PORT) across many iterations; at 329 announces 'fundamentally different approach' but executes the same loop and never re-architects; never diagnoses the runaway PID 6482 blocking its own verification. Ends still at 0/325.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows a couple of genuine subsystem revisions early (TS→JS build switch, adding SSR middleware, relocating plugin loading), which lifts it above the pure-patching anchor of 3. But once real divergence sets in — persistent 0/325 with servers failing — it never revisits an underlying design decision; it re-hypothesizes the same three suspected bugs and loops kill/rebuild/test for 70+ iterations without verifying anything or diagnosing the runaway process crippling its own feedback. Its one 'fundamentally different approach' declaration (step 329) is followed by the identical loop. That matches anchor 3's 'local fixes, never revisits the underlying cause,' nudged to 4 by the early build-strategy and SSR reworks, and clearly below the deliberate, re-verified foundational pivots of anchors 8-10.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Plans SSR middleware that generically matches routes to pages, loads modules via server.ssrLoadModule, executes getServerSideProps/getStaticProps, renders React, collects head — general framework mechanics, not per-fixture output hardcoding.

Repeatedly frames the core work as generic 'route matching and SSR rendering' / 'full SSR: route matching, page loading, React rendering, HTML generation' rather than special-casing individual fixture routes.

Describes a 'comprehensive SSR middleware' covering pages+app routers, dynamic route matching, API routes, after() — implementing the real Next.js contract inferred from reference source rather than test-specific hacks.
Extensive reading of next-shims.d.ts contracts and reference Next.js/plugin-rsc source to derive semantics before writing code, supporting general (not fixture-fitted) implementation.

Final submission summary describes generic subsystems (route matching, dynamic routes, head collection, after()) with no mention of the hidden-vs-visible gap, no stress-testing beyond visible tests, and no articulation of why it holds on unseen cases.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently implemented actual framework semantics — filesystem route matching, generic data-fetching execution, React rendering, dynamic routes — and never reached for fixture-specific shortcuts or hardcoded outputs, which places it clearly above anchor 3. But it never explicitly reasons about the stated 373-hidden-test gap, never frames the visible suite as a sample, and never stress-tests behaviors beyond what the fixtures exercise, so it falls short of anchor 8. This matches anchor 5: general, semantics-faithful implementation without demonstrated awareness of the sampling gap.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
